post.summary:
Built-in load test: the server plays synthetic viewers against its own
HTTP stack and reports measured capacity. Admin-only; refuses to start
while real streams are active.

RestartServer triggers a graceful shutdown; a process supervisor (Docker
`restart: unless-stopped`, systemd) then brings the server back up. Admin
only. Has no effect when the process is not supervised (bare run / dev).

streamingBps.description:
Measured streaming throughput: bytes actually written to stream/HLS/
download responses since the previous GetDashboard call, as bits/s.
-1 on the very first call (no previous sample to diff against).

streamingBytesTotal.description: Cumulative streaming bytes served since the server started.

activeSessionsBps.description:
Theoretical outgoing rate: the summed source bitrate of every active
play session - what the server would push if every client pulled at
full speed.

eveyCpuPercent.description:
The part of cpu_percent taken by Evey itself: the server and every
process it forked (ffmpeg, ffprobe). The rest is the host's other work.

v1DecodeThroughput.description: DecodeThroughput is one measured DECODE-only rate, per source codec.

skippedCandidates.description:
skipped_candidates counts titles the mkvgo scenario had to pass over
(not eligible for the on-demand packager).

viewerMix.description:
viewer_mix is the composition at the sustained tier, per viewer type
("mkvgo", "transcode", "natural") - the answer to "how many DIFFERENT
kinds of users at once".

segmentMsP95ByType.description:
segment_ms_p95_by_type breaks the p95 down per viewer type, so a slow
mkvgo path cannot hide behind slow transcodes (or vice versa).

mode.description: mode is the behavior axis this run used (see StartLoadTestRequest.mode).

segmentSloMsByType.description:
segment_slo_ms_by_type is the latency budget each path was JUDGED against.
The paths do not share a segment length (mkvgo packages on keyframe
boundaries, the ffmpeg ladder emits 3s segments), so they cannot share a
budget. segment_slo_ms above is only the loosest of these.

resources.description:
resources is what the server CONSUMED while sustaining that viewer count -
the evidence behind a cpu_saturated / memory_saturated stop_reason.

perViewerCost.description:
per_viewer_cost is what ONE more viewer costs, measured as the slope across
tiers rather than a naive total/viewers (which would charge the idle
server's own consumption to the viewers). Absent when fewer than two tiers
were measured.

resourceBaseline.description:
resource_baseline is what the server consumed BEFORE the first viewer
joined: the floor the per-viewer cost is read against.

throughputCeilingBytesPerSec.description:
throughput_ceiling_bytes_per_sec is the byte rate the server could not
exceed, set when stop_reason is throughput_saturated. On a media server this
is the usual ceiling - not the CPU, not the RAM, but how fast it can READ
the films - and no CPU or memory gauge can see it.

diskReadStarved.description:
disk_read_starved: the server pushed real traffic while the kernel's I/O
counter barely moved. Either the page cache served everything, or the media
do not live on a block device (a network share, a 9p/virtiofs mount) where
per-cgroup I/O accounting is simply blind. Zero read is NOT the same as no
disk activity, and the panel must not present it as a fact.

endpoint.description:
endpoint is the origin the viewers actually hit (the reverse proxy when it
was reachable, the server's own loopback otherwise). Runs against different
endpoints are not comparable.

diskReadCeilingBytesPerSec.description:
disk_read_ceiling_bytes_per_sec is how fast this box can READ its media,
measured directly by the run (several files, scattered offsets, read at
once - the shape of load an audience creates). On a direct-play server this
is usually the real ceiling, and the kernel cannot report it when the
library sits on anything but a plain block device.

diskCeilingAtReaders.description:
disk_ceiling_at_readers is the concurrency width at which that ceiling was
reached. Indispensable next to the figure above: a peak measured at 4
sequential readers says nothing about what 21 scrubbing viewers will get.

diskReadAtAudienceBytesPerSec.description:
disk_read_at_audience_bytes_per_sec is what the SAME storage delivered at the
concurrency the sustained audience actually imposes on it. This is the figure
the run was competing against; the ceiling above is what the hardware gives
under laboratory conditions production never sees.

Reporting only the ceiling is how a disk at its knees gets read as 40% busy.

tiers.description:
tiers is one row per audience size the run measured, smallest first: the
climb itself, not just the rung it stopped on. Read the per-viewer cost down
the rows and it either holds steady (the server is scaling) or bends upward
(it is not) - which a single headline figure cannot say.

harnessCpuFraction.description:
harness_cpu_fraction is the share of the measured CPU burned by the load
GENERATOR rather than by the server. Every CPU figure above already has it
subtracted. harness_cpu_measured is false when no profile could be taken, in
which case all the CPU is charged to the server (the pessimistic reading).

memCacheBytes.description:
mem_cache_bytes is the page cache the run accumulated by reading films. NOT
consumption: the kernel hands it straight back. Reported so an operator can
see why a naive memory gauge climbs to fill the box during a load test.

slowestDiskBytesPerSec.description:
slowest_disk_bytes_per_sec is what the WEAKEST drive delivered. A library
spread over several disks is not one big disk: each drive saturates on its
own, and the film a viewer picks decides which. This is what sets how bad it
gets when viewers happen to land on that drive.

disksProbed.description: disks_probed is how many distinct drives the library was found to span.

readAmplification.description:
read_amplification is how many bytes the DISK delivered per byte served -
what the hardware actually paid. Zero when the kernel cannot account the
reads (a library on a network share or a 9p/virtiofs mount).

appReadAmplification.description:
app_read_amplification is how many bytes the SERVER ASKED FOR per byte
served - the packager's own appetite, page cache or not.

The pair names the culprit, and the two have entirely different fixes:
  app 1.3 / disk 1.3 -> the code reads what it serves; nothing to win.
  app 2.5 / disk 2.5 -> the CODE traverses data it discards. Fix the packager.
  app 1.3 / disk 2.6 -> the KERNEL reads ahead into data nobody wanted. The
                        code is near-optimal; the fix is in HOW the file is
                        read, not in what it reads.
The disk figure alone leaves an operator guessing which of the three they
are looking at.

storageCollapsesAtReaders.description:
storage_collapses_at_readers is the number of concurrent readers past which
the storage stops merely plateauing and FALLS OVER - throughput halves or
worse, and a single read starts taking seconds. Zero when it never did.

When it is not zero it is the most important number in the report: on a
direct-play server it is roughly how many people can watch at once before
the STORAGE - not the CPU, not Evey - makes playback crawl. No CPU or memory
gauge shows any of this.

coldCache.description:
cold_cache is true when the run kept evicting the library from the page
cache (and the eviction actually landed): the figures were measured
against the storage, not the RAM. A warm and a cold run of the same box
are two different answers - never compare them as one.

sourceMix.description:
source_mix is what the run actually SERVED, per source class, counted as
each title was handed to a viewer. The candidate pool is drawn by duration
alone, so two runs on the same host land on different viewer counts purely
by codec draw - a verdict that cannot name what it decoded cannot be read.

storageFsType.description:
storage_fs_type names the filesystem type(s) the library's files sit on
("ext4", "fuse.mergerfs", "nfs4"...), comma-joined when several.

storageOpaque.description:
storage_opaque is true when one of those mounts hides the disks from the
server's kernel (a FUSE pool, a network or VM share): the disk counter
cannot see its reads, a cold-cache eviction stops at the mount and a pool
counts as one disk. The storage figures then describe the delivery path.

v1LoadTestReport.description:
LoadTestReport is what the box MEASURED, next to what the admission model
predicted - the panel shows both so the operator sees promises kept.

v1LoadTestResources.description:
LoadTestResources is what the box was actually spending. The figures come
from the server's own cgroup, so every ffmpeg it spawned is already counted;
served_bytes_per_sec is tallied by the viewers themselves (they reach the
server over loopback, where no NIC counter would see the traffic).

v1LoadTestSourceMix.description: LoadTestSourceMix is one source class and how many viewers were placed on it.

cpuPercentPerViewer.description:
cpu_percent_per_viewer / mem_bytes_per_viewer: this row's cost divided by its
headcount. The TREND down the table is what says whether the server is still
scaling.

v1LoadTestTierCost.description:
LoadTestTierCost is what ONE audience size cost the server: one row of the
report's table. Every CPU figure is the SERVER's share - the load generator's
own overhead has already been subtracted - and mem_used_bytes is anonymous
memory, never the page cache of the films being read.

serverLanguage.description:
server_language/server_region expose the server-wide defaults so the
SPA can render pre-auth routes (login, setup) in the admin-picked
language instead of falling back to navigator.language.

passwordRecoveryEnabled.description:
password_recovery_enabled lets the (unauthenticated) login page decide
whether to show the "Forgot password?" link. The same flag lives on the
admin-only SystemInfo; this is its public projection (it only reveals
whether SMTP + recovery are configured, no sensitive detail).

serverName.description:
server_name is the admin-chosen instance name (Server settings, default
"Evey"): the pre-auth screens (login, tab title) brand the instance with
it. Public projection of the same value /healthz advertises.

demoMode.description:
demo_mode says this is the public demo instance (EVEY_DEMO=1): the
clients show a banner and grey out what the server reports locked. The
server refuses the locked operations whether or not a client honours it.

serverName.description:
server_name is optional: blank keeps the default, otherwise it is
persisted as server.name (the admin settings key) and applied live.

baseUrl.description:
base_url was never read: the public URL is Remote access -> External URL
(EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL for the LAN one). Kept for wire compatibility only.

serverLanguage.description:
Optional: locale+region chosen during the wizard. Persisted as
server.language / server.region so new profiles inherit them.

v1SourceClass.description:
SourceClass is a decode workload: the source codec and the height it is
decoded at. See apptranscoding / transcoding.SourceClass.

scenario.description:
scenario is WHO the simulated viewers are: "transcode", "natural",
"mkvgo", the ratio mixes "light"/"balanced"/"heavy", or "mkvgo+N"
(N pinned transcodes then pure direct-play).

maxViewers.description: max_viewers caps the ramp; 0 = server default (12, sized for a weak NAS).

mode.description:
mode is HOW they behave: "" (ramp, default), "flash" (everyone arrives at
once - the sunday-evening stampede), "seek" (viewers jump around the
timeline - session churn), "endurance" (hold the tier for the duration -
slow-drift hunting).

durationSec.description:
duration_sec bounds the run; 0 = mode default (4min ramp/flash/seek,
30min endurance).

coldCache.description:
cold_cache keeps evicting the library's files from the OS page cache for
the whole run, so the server's reads hit the actual storage. A box whose
library fits in RAM otherwise measures its memory bus and overstates the
viewer count, sometimes by a factor of several. Cold measures the day the
library dwarfs the RAM; warm (the default) measures today. Both are true,
and the report says which one was measured.

path.description:
Representative path for this physical disk (the first library path that
resolved to it). Kept for backwards compatibility with older clients.

paths.description:
Every distinct library path that lives on this same physical disk (same
filesystem device id). Lets the UI group libraries per drive instead of
showing the same disk's capacity once per library.

videoSessions.description:
VideoSessions surfaces the AUTO-derived cap on concurrent VIDEO transcode
(encode, never copy/remux) sessions, the admin-overridden effective limit,
and how many are live right now - so the admin panel can show "why" a
number was chosen instead of a bare integer. Unset when no calibration
service is wired (e.g. a hand-built test server).

commit.description:
commit is the git SHA the running binary was built from, build_date its
RFC3339 build timestamp. `version` above is a branch or tag name and so
cannot identify a deployment: two images months apart both report
"beta-0.0.1-full". Both fields are the literal "unknown" - never blank -
when the build could not be stamped, so a client can tell "this server is
too old to answer" from "this build genuinely does not know".

derived.description:
derived is false when no usable calibration evidence existed and
auto_capacity fell back to the conservative default of 1.

v1VideoCapacityEvidence.description:
VideoCapacityEvidence is the "why" behind auto_capacity: the tallest
PASSING software bench rung the number was derived from.

v1VideoClassRungs.description:
VideoClassRungs is one ladder class's calibrated rung costs, for the admin
panel's per-pool breakdown. See apptranscoding.VideoCostModel.RungsFor.

classes.description:
classes is every ladder class billed against this pool that has usable
calibration evidence - "software" (+ "software-hdr"/"software-av1" when
benched) for the cpu pool, "hw" for the gpu pool.

v1VideoPool.description:
VideoPool is one resource pool's (cpu or gpu) admission budget and the
calibrated rung costs of the ladder class(es) billed against it. See
apptranscoding.ResourcePool / LadderClass.Pool.

bySource.description:
by_source prices this same rung for each source class the host measured.
cost/max_streams above are the source-agnostic figures the bench produced;
they answer "how many streams at this output height" only for the source
the bench decoded, which is why the breakdown exists. Empty when the host
has no decode evidence.

v1VideoRungFit.description:
VideoRungFit is one calibrated resolution rung's admission cost and how
many concurrent streams topping out at that height the host's budget
fits. See apptranscoding.VideoCostModel.Rungs.

budgetUsed.description:
budget_used / budget_total are the cost-model view of capacity: the
fraction of "one whole host" currently reserved by live streams, and the
budget new streams may spend (default 1.0). Both stay 0 / 0 when no cost
model is wired to the limiter - the panel then falls back to the
auto_capacity/active counter view above.

rungFits.description:
rung_fits is the per-resolution cost breakdown the budget above is
derived from - empty when no cost model is wired.

pools.description:
pools is the per-resource-pool view of the SAME budget: CPU (every
software ladder class) and, only when the host has a hw bench table
(see apptranscoding.VideoCostModel.Classes), a separate GPU pool. The
aggregate budget_used/budget_total above are the SUM across pools and
are misleading once two independent pools exist (e.g. a GPU-heavy box
shows "0.7/2" instead of "0.5/1 cpu, 0.2/1 gpu") - pools is the
authoritative breakdown; the fields above stay for older clients.

benchSource.description:
bench_source is the codec+height the encode rungs were DECODED from, and
decode_throughput the measured decode-only fps per codec. They are what
makes the rung costs interpretable: the same rung costs ~4x more fed by a
4K HEVC source than by a 1080p H.264 one. Unset on a host calibrated
before decode probing existed.

v1VideoSessionCapacity.description:
VideoSessionCapacity is the admin-facing view of the AUTO video-session cap
(derived from the boot benchmark), the effective limit actually enforced
(auto, possibly reduced by transcoding.max_video_sessions), and the live
count. See apptranscoding.AutoVideoSessionCapacity / ResolveVideoSessionLimit.

v1VideoSourceFit.description:
VideoSourceFit is one rung's cost for one SOURCE class - the answer to "how
many of these can I serve" once the thing being decoded is named.
